content: Staphylococcus aureus, commonly referred to as golden staph, is a spherical bacterium that frequently resides on human skin or in the nasal passages. Approximately 20–30% of the population are carriers of this bacterium. It is capable of causing a wide spectrum of diseases, ranging from minor skin infections, such as pimples, boils, impetigo, cellulitis, folliculitis, furuncles, carbuncles, and abscesses, to severe and potentially life-threatening conditions, including pneumonia, meningitis, osteomyelitis, endocarditis, toxic shock syndrome (TSS), and septicemia. It is a significant cause of infections in various tissues, including skin, soft tissue, respiratory tract, bones, joints, and wounds. Staphylococcus aureus is also one of the leading causes of hospital-acquired infections, particularly post-surgical wound infections. This bacterium was first identified in 1880 by Sir Alexander Ogston in Aberdeen, Scotland, in pus from surgical abscesses. In the United States alone, approximately 500,000 patients in hospitals acquire staphylococcal infections annually. Under the microscope, Staphylococcus aureus appears as clusters resembling grapes. It is a Gram-positive organism that forms large, round, golden-yellow colonies on blood agar plates, often exhibiting hemolysis. The golden coloration of its colonies is the origin of its name, as aureus means golden in Latin. Staphylococcus aureus is a facultative anaerobe and an opportunistic pathogen. It is catalase-positive, meaning it produces the enzyme catalase, which converts hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. This property helps distinguish it from other bacteria, such as streptococci and enterococci. Additionally, most strains of Staphylococcus aureus are coagulase-positive, producing the enzyme coagulase, which facilitates clot formation. Accurate identification is critical, as Staphylococcus aureus is more aggressive and often resistant to antibiotics compared to other staphylococcal species. Staphylococcus aureus can exist as a commensal organism on human skin, in the nose, and occasionally in the throat without causing disease. In such cases, treatment is not always necessary, as eradication may be ineffective and recolonization can occur. The bacterium can also survive on domestic animals, such as dogs, cats, and horses, and is known to cause bumblefoot in chickens. It can persist on dry environmental surfaces for hours, although the role of environmental surfaces in its transmission remains debated. Staphylococcus aureus can harbor virulence factors, such as the Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL), which enhance its ability to cause disease. When the skin or mucosal barriers are breached, the bacterium can invade deeper tissues, leading to infections such as furuncles (boils) and carbuncles (clusters of boils). In infants, it can cause a severe condition known as staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS). Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected wounds, skin-to-skin contact, or contact with contaminated objects like towels, clothing, or sports equipment. Deep-seated infections, such as septic arthritis in individuals with prosthetic joints, staphylococcal endocarditis, and pneumonia, can be particularly severe and rapidly progressive. Patients with atopic dermatitis are especially vulnerable to Staphylococcus aureus colonization and infection. The bacterium frequently complicates this condition, particularly in areas such as the armpits, scalp, and hair follicles. Large pimples in these regions, when ruptured, can exacerbate the infection. Certain strains of Staphylococcus aureus produce toxins that cause toxic shock syndrome (TSS). These strains produce toxic shock syndrome toxin (TSST-1), which is associated with tampon use. Other strains produce enterotoxins that lead to staphylococcal food poisoning. In dairy cows, Staphylococcus aureus is a major cause of mastitis, with its large capsule providing protection against the cow's immune defenses. Staphylococcus aureus produces a variety of toxins that contribute to its virulence. These toxins are categorized into three groups. Pyrogenic toxin superantigens (PTSAgs), such as TSST-1, are responsible for toxic shock syndrome. Staphylococcal enterotoxins, which are also part of this group, cause food poisoning. Exfoliative toxins are implicated in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS), particularly in infants and young children, and can lead to outbreaks in hospital nurseries. These toxins have protease activity, which causes the skin peeling characteristic of SSSS. Other toxins, such as alpha-toxin, beta-toxin, delta-toxin, and bicomponent toxins like Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL), target cell membranes. PVL is associated with severe necrotizing pneumonia, particularly in children. The genes encoding PVL are carried on a bacteriophage found in community-associated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (CA-MRSA) strains. The golden pigmentation of Staphylococcus aureus, produced by carotenoid compounds, may play a role in its virulence. In experiments, pigmented strains were more likely to survive attacks by human neutrophils and caused more persistent abscesses in animal models. In contrast, unpigmented strains were more easily eradicated and caused less severe infections. These findings suggest that the yellow pigment enhances the bacterium's ability to evade the immune system. Drugs targeting the production of these carotenoids may weaken the bacterium and restore its susceptibility to antibiotics.
